name: Bird poop facial

lead: The bird poop facial, or uguisu no fun, is a Japanese-origin treatment using powdered droppings of the Japanese bush warbler (called nightingale in marketing). It is offered as a way to brighten and smooth skin and tighten pores.

Promoters credit it to geisha and kabuki performers, who are said to have used it to remove makeup and whiten the face. Modern interest was fuelled by press reports in the late 2000s that Victoria Beckham used it.

paras: Spas mix the sterilised powder with rice bran or water into a paste, apply it as a mask for a short time or as part of a longer facial, then rinse. Treatments may also include steaming, massage and a collagen mask.

Bird droppings in general can host pathogens such as the fungus behind histoplasmosis, which is why commercial powders are sun-dried, UV-sterilised and ground. No published trials test the facial, and skeptical bloggers have questioned the claimed mechanism.

angle.text: Proponents say the mask lifts dullness, clears blemishes and tightens pores, similar to an exfoliating facial. One reviewer of a Dubai session said her skin felt non-greasy with a glow lasting more than a week, but was unsure it looked lighter.

lead: The bird poop facial, known in Japan as uguisu no fun, uses powdered droppings from the Japanese bush warbler, marketed in English as nightingale droppings.[1] It is offered as a way to brighten, exfoliate and smooth skin and minimise pores.[2]

Sellers say Japanese women used the powder for centuries, first as a fabric stain remover and then as a skin whitener adopted by geisha and noblewomen.[1] A dermatologist quoted by AOL said 18th-century geishas and kabuki actors used it to remove heavy makeup and whiten their faces.[2] A news report on a Dubai clinic traced the earliest written reference to a 1933 book and credited its modern revival largely to Victoria Beckham, whose use has been reported by tabloids and was presented by a Japanese beauty company as a claim.[1][3]
No clinical studies of the facial exist. Commentators have disputed the marketing explanation that guanine acts as an enzyme.[4]
infobox: Sterilised bird dropping powder, often with rice bran

paras: Per a 2009 product feature, the powder is made by sun-drying droppings for about two weeks, sterilising them with ultraviolet light and grinding them fine; a small amount is mixed with water, spread on the face and rinsed after a few minutes.[1] At a Dubai clinic the paste was powder with Japanese rice bran, followed by steam, extraction, high-frequency current, a camellia oil massage and a collagen mask; the powder was imported from Japan from birds raised in sanitary conditions.[3]

Brand and press accounts place the practice in geisha culture and in 17th and 18th century Japan, though a critical commenter noted that geisha used it mainly as white face paint.[1][2][3][4] The Beckham reports around 2008-2009 brought it to Western media, and spas in the US and Middle East later offered it.[1][3][4]

Dermatologist Melissa Kanchanapoomi Levin explained that droppings contain urea, which helps skin retain moisture, and guanine, said to give a luminous quality; proponents add that it clears acne and smooths skin.[2] A 2010 blog post on a US spa's marketing noted that guanine is a nitrogenous base rather than an enzyme and questioned why nightingale rather than pigeon droppings are used.[4]

Bird guano is a habitat of Histoplasma capsulatum, a fungus that causes infection, particularly serious for immunocompromised people.[5] Commenters have also raised parrot-borne psittacosis.[4] Commercial powders are described as sterilised.[1][3]

lore.intro: The treatment circulates mainly as a celebrity and spa curiosity rather than a forum protocol.[3]
